questions.e: 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (or credit-equivalent of off-balance-sheet exposure) must go to priority sectors, with sub-targets: 18% agriculture (10% to small/marginal farmers), 7.5% micro enterprises.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: PMFBY farmer premium for kharif crops is:
questions.e: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana: farmer pays 2% (kharif), 1.5% (rabi), 5% (commercial/horticultural); Centre and State share the balance actuarial premium.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: NABARD launched the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme as a pilot in:
questions.e: The SHG-Bank Linkage pilot began in 1991-92 with NABARD refinance support and grew into the world's largest microfinance programme.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: RIDF is maintained with:
questions.e: The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund with NABARD absorbs banks' priority-sector shortfalls, financing rural roads, irrigation and agri-infrastructure.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: MUDRA loan categories Shishu, Kishore, Tarun cover loans up to:
o: Rs.1 lakh; Rs.5 lakh; Rs.20 lakh
questions.e: Shishu (up to Rs.50,000), Kishore (Rs.50,001-5 lakh), Tarun (Rs.5-10 lakh); Tarun Plus extends to Rs.20 lakh for successful Tarun borrowers.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The scale of finance for crop loans is fixed by:
questions.e: DLTCs (with agri experts) fix per-acre scales of finance by crop and district — the basis for KCC limits.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Joint Liability Groups (JLGs) typically have:
questions.e: JLGs of 4-10 members (often tenant/sharecropper farmers) get individual or group loans without collateral, with mutual guarantee substituting for security.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: PM-KISAN provides income support of:
o: Rs.6,000 per year in three instalments
questions.e: PM-KISAN pays Rs.6,000/year in three Rs.2,000 instalments via DBT to eligible farmer families — a staple exam fact.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Locke's goal-setting theory states that:
o: Specific, challenging goals with feedback improve performance
questions.e: Edwin Locke found specific, difficult-but-accepted goals with feedback outperform 'do your best' exhortations — the basis of modern target-setting.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The Job Characteristics Model (Hackman & Oldham) includes all EXCEPT:
questions.e: The five core dimensions are skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback — producing meaningfulness, responsibility and knowledge of results. Salary is not one.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Bipartite settlements in banks are negotiated between:
questions.e: The Indian Banks' Association negotiates bipartite settlements with unions (AIBEA, NCBE, AIBOC etc.) fixing PSB pay — the 12th BPS covers 2022-27.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act applies to establishments with:
questions.e: The 1946 Act requires standing orders (service conditions) in industrial establishments with 50+ workers (threshold varies by state amendment; the central Code raises it).

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: A domestic enquiry against a charge-sheeted employee must follow:
questions.e: Charge sheet, reasonable opportunity to be heard, unbiased enquiry officer, and reasoned findings — violating natural justice vitiates the dismissal.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: HR analytics in banks is used for:
o: Attrition prediction and hiring quality measurement
questions.e: People analytics applies data to attrition modelling, recruitment ROI, training effectiveness and succession risk — the emerging HRM frontier.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Mentoring differs from coaching in that mentoring is:
questions.e: Coaching is short-term performance-focused; mentoring is a longer developmental relationship where a senior guides career growth — both are management-development tools.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Competency mapping identifies:
o: Knowledge, skills and behaviours needed for roles
questions.e: Competency mapping profiles the KSAOs (knowledge, skills, abilities, other attributes) each role needs, feeding recruitment, training and succession planning.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The balanced scorecard's four perspectives are:
o: Financial, customer, internal process, learning & growth
questions.e: Kaplan and Norton's scorecard balances financial, customer, internal-process and learning-and-growth measures — increasingly applied to HR and bank performance.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Grievance handling's first step in the model procedure is:
o: Raising the grievance with the immediate supervisor
questions.e: The 1958 model grievance procedure starts with the aggrieved employee approaching the immediate supervisor, escalating up defined levels within time limits.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: INFINET is:
o: RBI's closed user group network for banks/FIs
questions.e: The Indian Financial Network is RBI's secure closed-user-group communication backbone for the banking and financial sector.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: UPI per-transaction limit is generally:
o: Rs.1 lakh (Rs.5 lakh for specified categories)
questions.e: Standard UPI cap is Rs.1 lakh per transaction; RBI raised it to Rs.5 lakh for specified merchants like hospitals, education and IPOs.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The NEFT system in India is operated by:
questions.e: NEFT is owned and operated by the RBI; it settles in half-hourly batches on a deferred net settlement basis, 24x7.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: RBI's e-rupee (CBDC) pilots cover:
questions.e: RBI pilots both wholesale CBDC (settlement) and retail CBDC (public digital cash) — programmable, token-based digital rupee.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: RBI's data-localisation circular (2018) requires:
o: Payment data stored only in India
questions.e: All payment-system data must be stored in systems located only in India — a landmark compliance requirement for global card networks and fintechs.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: CERT-In's role in banking cybersecurity is:
o: National nodal agency for incident response; banks report breaches
questions.e: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team coordinates incident response; RBI's Cyber Security Framework mandates banks report incidents to CERT-In and RBI promptly.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Two-factor authentication for card-not-present transactions was mandated by RBI to curb:
questions.e: RBI's additional factor of authentication (OTP/password) for online card transactions sharply cut card-not-present fraud in India.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: An Account Aggregator:
o: Shares consented financial data between FIPs and FIUs
questions.e: NBFC-AAs enable consented, encrypted sharing of financial data (bank statements, GST, investments) from providers to users — powering digital lending underwriting.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Digital Lending Guidelines (2022) require:
o: APR disclosure, cooling-off period and direct bank-credit of loans
questions.e: RBI's digital-lending norms mandate key fact statements with APR, a cooling-off/look-up period, and disbursal directly to borrower accounts — banning auto-limit hikes without consent.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: ISO 27001 is a standard for:
questions.e: ISO/IEC 27001 specifies an Information Security Management System — the benchmark banks cite for IS controls, alongside COBIT for IT governance.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Expected Shortfall differs from VaR because it:
o: Averages losses beyond the VaR threshold
questions.e: Expected shortfall (conditional VaR) = average loss given VaR is exceeded — capturing tail severity that VaR misses. Basel's FRTB uses ES at 97.5%.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The Standardised Measurement Approach for operational risk uses:
o: Business Indicator x Internal Loss Multiplier
questions.e: SMA: capital = Business Indicator Component (based on income/asset proxies) multiplied by the Internal Loss Multiplier reflecting the bank's loss history.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: RAROC hurdle rate is typically the bank's:
questions.e: RAROC is compared against the cost of equity (target return) — deals earning above it create shareholder value; below it destroy value.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Wrong-way risk arises when:
o: Counterparty default correlates positively with exposure
questions.e: Wrong-way risk = exposure to a counterparty rises exactly when its credit quality falls — e.g., selling protection on a bank to that same bank's affiliate.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: A credit rating downgrade of a corporate borrower from AA to BBB under the standardised approach:
questions.e: Risk weights rise as ratings fall (AAA 20%, A 50%, BBB 100%, below BB 150%) — downgrades directly increase RWA and capital needs.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Liquidity risk in the trading book is addressed by:
o: Liquidity horizons in FRTB market-risk capital
questions.e: Basel's FRTB assigns liquidity horizons (10-120 days) by asset class — illiquid positions attract higher ES-based capital, unlike the old uniform 10-day VaR.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The risk that models are wrong is called:
questions.e: Model risk — errors in design, data or use of quantitative models — gets dedicated governance: validation, challenger models and use-tests, per RBI guidance.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: In stress testing, reverse stress tests:
o: Find scenarios that would break the bank
questions.e: Reverse stress tests start from failure (e.g., capital breach) and work backwards to find the shocks causing it — revealing hidden vulnerabilities.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Concentration risk to a single sector is measured by:
questions.e: The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (sum of squared shares) quantifies portfolio concentration — higher HHI means riskier concentration in few borrowers/sectors.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Economic capital is calibrated to:
questions.e: Economic capital = unexpected loss at the bank's chosen confidence (often tied to its target rating) — the internal view that may exceed regulatory minimums.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The MPC's inflation target is set by:
o: The Central Government in consultation with RBI
questions.e: The government notifies the 4% (+/-2%) CPI target every five years in consultation with RBI — the statutory anchor of flexible inflation targeting.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Sterilisation by RBI means:
questions.e: When RBI buys dollars (injecting rupees), it sterilises by selling G-secs via OMO or MSS bonds — keeping money supply on target.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Primary dealers' main obligation is:
questions.e: PDs must bid for and underwrite government securities auctions and provide two-way quotes — RBI's conduit for monetary transmission in bond markets.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The FSDC is chaired by:
questions.e: The Financial Stability and Development Council, apex forum for inter-regulatory coordination, is chaired by the Finance Minister with all regulators as members.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: Scale-Based Regulation (SBR) for NBFCs has how many layers?
questions.e: SBR (Oct 2021): base, middle, upper and top layers — regulatory intensity rises with size and systemic importance; upper-layer NBFCs face bank-like norms.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The repo rate as of RBI's August 2026 review was:
questions.e: After the easing cycle, RBI held the repo at 5.25% in August 2026 (SDF 5.00%, MSF/Bank Rate 5.50%). Verify the latest MPC outcome before the exam.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: External benchmark (EBLR) for floating retail/MSME loans is linked to:
questions.e: Since October 2019, floating-rate retail and MSME loans must link to an external benchmark — mostly the RBI policy repo rate — for faster transmission.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: India's forex reserves are managed with the hierarchy:
questions.e: RBI manages reserves for safety first, then liquidity, then return — intervention aims only to curb undue volatility, not to target a level.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: OSMOS refers to:
questions.e: Off-site Surveillance and Monitoring System collects supervisory returns from banks — RBI's early-warning radar between on-site inspections.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: The Financial Stability Report is published by RBI:
questions.e: RBI's FSR (June and December) assesses systemic risks, banking-sector resilience and stress-test results — prime current-affairs material for the Central Banking elective.

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: For the CAIIB November-December 2026 cycle, IIBF's notified registration window and paper schedule are:
o: Registration 13 September-1 October 2026; papers 6-27 December 2026 (ABM 6 Dec, BFM 12 Dec, ABFM 13 Dec, BRBL 20 Dec, elective 27 Dec)
Registration 1-30 November 2026; all papers on a single day
Registration closed on 31 August 2026; exams in January 2027
Registration throughout December 2026; papers in March 2027
questions.e: IIBF opened registration for the CAIIB Nov-Dec 2026 cycle from 13 September to 1 October 2026. The papers run 6-27 December 2026: Advanced Bank Management (6 Dec), Bank Financial Management (12 Dec), Advanced Business & Financial Management (13 Dec), Banking Regulations & Business Laws (20 Dec), and the elective paper (27 Dec).

questions.subject: CAIIB
questions.q: As notified by IIBF for the CAIIB November-December 2026 cycle, the examination fee is:
o: Rs 5,000 plus GST for the first attempt; Rs 1,300 plus GST per subsequent attempt
questions.e: First attempt: Rs 5,000 + GST; second to fifth attempts: Rs 1,300 + GST per attempt. Late registration attracts Rs 100 (20-26 September) or Rs 200 (27 September-1 October). The fee is non-refundable and payable online.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 under which legislation?
questions.e: The RBI was constituted on 1 April 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 governs banking companies, not the RBI's creation. The RBI was nationalised on 1 January 1949.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which of the following IS a function of the Reserve Bank of India?
o: Accepting deposits from the general public
Acting as lender of last resort to banks
questions.e: The RBI is the lender of last resort, note-issuing authority, banker to governments and regulator of banks — it does not accept public deposits or run branches.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: As per the August 2026 monetary policy review, the repo rate stands at:
questions.e: The August 2026 MPC review kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25% with a neutral stance. SDF was 5.00%, while MSF and Bank Rate were 5.50%. These rates are high-frequency exam anchors.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) as of August 2026 is:
questions.e: CRR was 3.00% in the August 2026 review. CRR is the share of net demand and time liabilities banks must hold as cash balances with the RBI, earning no interest. SLR stood at 18.00%.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Statutory Liquidity Ratio requires banks to maintain liquid assets in the form of:
o: Cash, gold and approved government securities
questions.e: SLR (18.00% as of August 2026) must be maintained in cash, gold or unencumbered approved securities, mainly government securities. It is a quantitative tool that also ensures bank solvency.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The inflation target set for the Monetary Policy Committee under the RBI Act is:
o: 4% CPI inflation with a tolerance band of ±2%
questions.e: The government notifies a 4% CPI target with ±2% tolerance; the 6-member MPC sets the repo rate to achieve it.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The inflation target assigned to the RBI under the monetary policy framework is:
questions.e: The Government notified a CPI inflation target of 4% with an upper tolerance of 6% and lower tolerance of 2%. If inflation stays outside the band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must explain to the Government.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which instrument is used by the RBI to inject or absorb durable liquidity through purchase/sale of government securities?
questions.e: OMO involves outright purchase or sale of government securities to durably inject or absorb liquidity. The Bank Rate is the rate at which RBI rediscounts bills; moral suasion and selective controls are qualitative tools.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under the 'One State–One RRB' consolidation, the number of Regional Rural Banks was reduced from 43 to 28 with effect from:
questions.e: The fourth phase of RRB amalgamation under Section 23A(1) of the RRB Act, 1976 took effect on 1 May 2025, reducing RRBs from 43 to 28 across 26 states and 2 UTs, each with authorised capital of ₹2,000 crore.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The shareholding pattern of a Regional Rural Bank among Central Government, sponsor bank and State Government is:
questions.e: RRBs are owned 50% by the Central Government, 35% by the sponsor bank and 15% by the State Government concerned. RRBs were first established under the ordinance of 26 September 1975.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Small Finance Banks must extend what percentage of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit to the priority sector?
questions.e: SFBs (and RRBs) have a priority-sector target of 75% of ANBC or CEOBE, whichever is higher — much higher than the 40% for domestic commercial banks, reflecting their inclusion mandate.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which of the following can a Payments Bank NOT do?
questions.e: Payments Banks may accept demand deposits (up to the prescribed per-customer limit) and offer remittance and debit cards, but they are prohibited from lending. They must invest most balances in government securities.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Deposits with NBFCs are:
o: Insured up to ₹1 lakh by DICGC
Insured up to ₹5 lakh by DICGC
questions.e: DICGC insures deposits of banks only, up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank. NBFC deposits carry no DICGC cover — a classic exam trap distinguishing banks from NBFCs.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The DICGC insures bank deposits up to what amount per depositor per bank?
questions.e: The cover was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh in February 2020. It applies per depositor per bank across all branches, covering savings, fixed, current and recurring deposits.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: NABARD was established on 12 July 1982 on the recommendation of which committee?
questions.e: NABARD was set up on 12 July 1982 under the NABARD Act, 1981 on the Shivaraman Committee's recommendation, taking over the RBI's agricultural credit functions. The Narasimham Committees dealt with banking-sector reforms.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: SIDBI, the principal financial institution for MSME promotion, was established on:
questions.e: SIDBI was established on 2 April 1990 under an Act of Parliament as the principal institution for promotion, financing and development of MSMEs. IFCI (1948) was the first DFI; EXIM Bank dates to 1982.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The first Development Financial Institution of India was:
questions.e: The Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI), set up on 1 July 1948, was India's first DFI. IDBI began in 1964 as an RBI subsidiary; ICICI was set up in 1955 with World Bank support.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: SEBI became a statutory body in 1992 under:
questions.e: SEBI was first set up in April 1988 as a non-statutory body and given statutory powers through the SEBI Act, 1992 (30 January 1992). It regulates the securities market and protects investors.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The insurance regulator IRDAI was constituted under:
questions.e: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority was set up under the IRDA Act, 1999, opening the insurance sector to private players. PFRDA (pensions) became statutory in 2013.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which money-market instrument is issued by the Government of India with maturities of 91, 182 and 364 days?
questions.e: T-Bills are zero-coupon sovereign instruments issued at a discount in 91, 182 and 364-day maturities. Commercial paper is issued by corporates; CDs are issued by banks/FIs; call money is overnight inter-bank borrowing.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The minimum denomination for Commercial Paper in India is:
questions.e: Commercial Paper is issued in minimum denominations of ₹5 lakh (and multiples thereof) by highly rated corporates. Certificates of Deposit have a minimum of ₹1 lakh.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The National Stock Exchange (NSE) commenced operations in the capital market segment in:
questions.e: NSE was incorporated in 1992 and began operations — wholesale debt in June 1994 and capital market in November 1994. BSE, Asia's oldest exchange, dates to 1875.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which of the following is a qualitative (selective) instrument of monetary policy?
o: Margin requirements on advances against securities
questions.e: Margin requirements, credit rationing and moral suasion are qualitative/selective tools targeting specific sectors. CRR, OMO and the repo rate are quantitative tools affecting overall credit volume.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Bank Rate as of August 2026 is:
questions.e: Bank Rate stood at 5.50% in August 2026, aligned with the MSF rate. The Bank Rate is the rate at which the RBI rediscounts bills of exchange; penal interest is often linked to it.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), introduced by the RBI in May 2011, is:
o: An overnight emergency borrowing window against approved securities
questions.e: MSF was introduced in May 2011, allowing banks to borrow overnight from the RBI against approved securities up to a prescribed limit of NDTL at a penal rate above the repo rate. It acts as a safety valve when inter-bank liquidity dries up.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) rate as of August 2026 is:
questions.e: The August 2026 MPC held the repo rate at 5.25% with a neutral stance: SDF (floor of the corridor) stayed at 5.00%, MSF and Bank Rate at 5.50%.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Priority sector target for domestic scheduled commercial banks is:
o: 40% of ANBC or CEOBE, whichever is higher
questions.e: Domestic SCBs (and foreign banks with 20+ branches) must direct 40% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit or Credit Equivalent of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher, to priority sectors. 18% is only the agriculture sub-target.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches in India have a priority-sector target of:
o: 40% of ANBC, with up to 32% as export credit
questions.e: All foreign banks face a 40% overall PSL target; those with under 20 branches may count up to 32% of ANBC as export credit, with at least 8% to other priority sectors, reflecting their limited rural reach.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 primarily:
o: Brought urban co-operative banks substantially under RBI supervision
questions.e: The 2020 amendment extended RBI's regulatory powers (supersession of boards, reconstruction schemes, etc.) to urban co-operative banks after the PMC Bank episode. Bank nationalisation was 1969/1980.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which of the following deposits is NOT covered by DICGC insurance?
o: Deposits of a foreign government held in India
questions.e: Deposits of foreign governments, the Central/State Governments, and inter-bank deposits are excluded from DICGC cover. Individual, company, savings, fixed and recurring deposits are all insured up to ₹5 lakh.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The first bank established in India was:
questions.e: The Bank of Hindustan, set up in 1770 by Alexander & Co. in Calcutta, was India's first bank. The Presidency Bank of Bengal came in 1806; Allahabad Bank (1865) is the oldest surviving joint-stock bank.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Imperial Bank of India was formed in 1921 by amalgamating:
o: The three Presidency Banks of Bengal, Bombay and Madras
questions.e: The Bank of Bengal (1806), Bank of Bombay (1840) and Bank of Madras (1843) were merged in 1921 to form the Imperial Bank of India, which became SBI on 1 July 1955.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: State Bank of India was constituted on 1 July 1955 under:
questions.e: The Imperial Bank of India was converted into SBI on 1 July 1955 under the State Bank of India Act, 1955, on the All-India Rural Credit Survey Committee's recommendation. SBI's associate banks later merged into it (2017).

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The 14 major banks were nationalised on:
questions.e: Fourteen banks with deposits over ₹50 crore were nationalised on 19 July 1969. Six more followed on 15 April 1980. The RBI was nationalised on 1 January 1949.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Narasimham Committee-II (1998) is best known for recommending:
o: Merger of strong banks and 'narrow banking' for weak ones
questions.e: Narasimham-II (Committee on Banking Sector Reforms, 1998) recommended consolidation through mergers of strong banks and narrow banking for weak banks.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Lead Bank Scheme was introduced in 1969 on the recommendation of:
o: The Gadgil Study Group / Nariman Committee
questions.e: The Lead Bank Scheme (1969) assigned districts to banks for coordinated credit planning, based on the Gadgil Study Group and Nariman Committee. The Tandon/Chore committees dealt with working-capital assessment.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Differential Rate of Interest (DRI) scheme advances are given at:
questions.e: Under DRI, banks lend at 4% p.a. to weaker sections (landless labourers, SC/ST, etc.) up to prescribed limits, with at least 1% of previous year's advances earmarked. It is a directed-lending inclusion tool.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Service Area Approach, assigning villages to bank branches, was introduced in:
questions.e: The Service Area Approach (1989) allotted 15–25 villages to each rural/semi-urban branch for planned credit delivery and annual credit plans, complementing the Lead Bank Scheme.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which institution refinances RRBs, co-operative banks and promotes rural development?
questions.e: NABARD refinances rural credit institutions, inspects RRBs and co-operative banks, and promotes rural development. SIDBI serves MSMEs; EXIM Bank handles foreign trade finance; NHB is for housing finance.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units (CGFMU) supports:
o: Collateral-free MUDRA loans up to ₹20 lakh
questions.e: CGFMU, managed through NCGTC, guarantees MUDRA loans; coverage was extended to ₹20 lakh alongside the Tarun Plus category (effective 24 October 2024). PMMY itself was launched 8 April 2015.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: India Post Payments Bank was launched on:
questions.e: IPPB was launched on 1 September 2018, leveraging the postal network for doorstep banking. UPI launched 11 April 2016; PMJDY on 28 August 2014; MUDRA on 8 April 2015.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The first Small Finance Bank to commence operations (April 2016) was:
questions.e: Capital Small Finance Bank (Punjab) was the first SFB to start operations in April 2016. Airtel Payments Bank was the first payments bank (pilot November 2016). SFB guidelines were issued in November 2014.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Local Area Banks (first licensed in 1996) were set up to mobilise rural savings for local lending with what minimum capital?
questions.e: Local Area Banks were conceived to mobilise rural and semi-urban savings for local lending, with ₹5 crore as the minimum capital requirement at inception. Only a handful, such as Coastal Local Area Bank, continue to operate.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The largest component of a commercial bank's liabilities is typically:
questions.e: Deposits (demand + time) form 80%+ of a bank's liabilities — banks are deposit-funded institutions. Borrowings, capital and other liabilities are much smaller in comparison.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A bank's Net Interest Margin (NIM) is:
o: Net interest income divided by average earning assets
Total income divided by total assets
Profit after tax divided by equity
questions.e: NIM = (interest earned − interest expended) ÷ average earning assets, measuring core lending profitability. ROA uses profit/total assets; ROE uses profit/equity.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The CASA ratio of a bank refers to:
o: Current and Savings deposits as a percentage of total deposits
questions.e: CASA = low-cost demand deposits ÷ total deposits. A higher CASA lowers the cost of funds and widens NIM — hence banks chase CASA aggressively.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: In June 2024 the RBI redefined bulk deposits for SCBs (excl. RRBs) and SFBs as:
o: Single rupee term deposits of ₹3 crore and above
Single rupee term deposits of ₹1 crore and above
Aggregate deposits of ₹10 crore and above
Single rupee term deposits of ₹2 crore and above
questions.e: On 7 June 2024 the RBI raised the bulk-deposit threshold from ₹2 crore to ₹3 crore for SCBs (excl. RRBs) and SFBs; for RRBs and Local Area Banks it is ₹1 crore. Banks may offer differential, even non-callable, rates on bulk deposits.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The interest on savings bank deposits in India is:
o: Linked to the repo rate mandatorily
Deregulated since October 2011; banks set their own rates
questions.e: The RBI deregulated savings deposit interest rates on 25 October 2011. Banks now set their own rates (many tier them by balance), though most cluster near the old 3–3.5% for small balances.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Treasury Bills are issued in India by:
o: The RBI on behalf of the Government of India
questions.e: T-Bills are sovereign short-term instruments issued through RBI auctions. They are zero-coupon, issued at a discount and redeemed at face value — the discount is the investor's return.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The call money market deals in:
questions.e: Call money is overnight (1 day); notice money is 2–14 days; term money exceeds 14 days. Only banks and primary dealers participate, managing day-to-day liquidity mismatches.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The banker–customer relationship in a deposit account is primarily that of:
questions.e: In a deposit account the bank owes the balance to the customer, making the bank the debtor and the customer the creditor. In a loan account this is reversed. Trustee, agency and bailment arise only from specific services like safe custody or cheque collection.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The banker's general lien is provided under which section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?
questions.e: Section 171 gives bankers a general lien over goods and securities bailed to them for the general balance of account. It does not extend to valuables kept for safe custody or to securities earmarked for a special purpose.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The banker's right of set-off means:
o: Freezing accounts on a court order
Charging penal interest on overdue loans
Combining accounts to adjust a debit balance against a credit balance
questions.e: Set-off lets a bank combine the customer's accounts in the same right and set a credit balance against a debit balance, after giving due notice. The accounts must be in the same name and capacity.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The rule in Clayton's case (Devaynes v Noble) applies to:
o: Appropriation of payments to the earliest debt when the debtor does not specify
questions.e: Under Sections 59–61 of the Indian Contract Act, if the debtor does not indicate appropriation, the creditor may apply it to any lawful debt; Clayton's rule defaults to the earliest debt in running accounts.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A garnishee order under Order 21 Rule 46 of the Civil Procedure Code attaches:
o: Debts owed by a third party (garnishee) to the judgment debtor
The future salary of any employee
questions.e: The order attaches debts due from the garnishee (e.g., a bank holding the debtor's deposits) to the judgment debtor, barring the garnishee from paying the debtor.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The bank's duty of secrecy does NOT apply when disclosure is:
o: Compelled by law, e.g. a court order or tax authority
questions.e: The duty of secrecy has four recognised exceptions: legal compulsion, the bank's own interest (e.g. suing the customer), public interest, and the customer's express or implied consent.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A mandate given by a customer to a third party to operate the account lapses on:
o: The death, insolvency or insanity of the customer
questions.e: A mandate is an agency; like any agency it terminates on the principal's death, insanity or insolvency. If the bank pays under a mandate without notice of death, it is protected.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: In an 'either or survivor' joint account, on the death of one holder the balance:
o: Is frozen until probate in all cases
Goes to the legal heirs only
Passes to the survivor(s) as per the mandate
questions.e: Under an either-or-survivor mandate the survivor takes the balance outside succession, as a contractual arrangement with the bank. Legal heirs may still claim against the survivor, but the bank is discharged by paying the survivor.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A minor can open and operate a savings account:
o: If above the prescribed age and able to operate, per RBI's minor-account directions
Only through a court-appointed guardian in all cases
questions.e: Minors above the prescribed age may open and operate savings accounts independently; younger minors operate through natural/legal guardians. The RBI's 2025 directions liberalised minor accounts, including internet banking with safeguards.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which of these is an Officially Valid Document (OVD) for KYC?
o: PAN card alone for address proof
questions.e: OVDs are: passport, driving licence, proof of possession of Aadhaar, Voter's ID, NREGA job card, and NPR letter. PAN is not an OVD (it lacks address); utility bills are only supporting documents.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR), where banks upload KYC records of customers, is operated by:
questions.e: CKYCR is maintained by CERSAI; reporting entities upload KYC data so a customer KYCed once need not repeat the process elsewhere.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Periodic KYC updation for medium-risk customers is due every:
questions.e: The risk-based cycle is 2/8/10 years for high/medium/low-risk customers. For low-risk customers with no change, banks may use digital self-declaration; the 2025 amendment gave low-risk customers whose KYC fell due time until June 2026.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Periodic KYC updation for low-risk customers is due every:
questions.e: Low-risk customers need KYC updation once in 10 years. Under the June 2025 RBI amendment, banks must send at least three advance intimations (one by letter) before the due date and three reminders after.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 came into force on:
questions.e: PMLA was enacted in 2002 but enforced from 1 July 2005. It mandates KYC, record-keeping and reporting of suspicious transactions to FIU-IND by banks and financial institutions.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Suspicious transactions detected by banks must be reported to:
questions.e: The Financial Intelligence Unit–India receives Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) and Cash Transaction Reports (CTRs, for cash transactions of ₹10 lakh and above in a month) from reporting entities.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The CKYCR identifier issued to a customer is:
questions.e: The Central KYC Records Registry assigns a 14-digit CKYC identifier so that KYC completed once can be reused across regulated entities, avoiding repeated document submission.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Video-based Customer Identification Process (V-CIP) is:
questions.e: The RBI permits V-CIP as an alternative to face-to-face onboarding, with prescribed safeguards like live location capture and authorised-officer conduct of the video call.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account (BSBDA) is characterised by:
o: No minimum balance with a cap on free withdrawals
questions.e: BSBDA is the no-frills account: zero minimum balance, no charge for non-operation, and a limited number of free withdrawals per month (usually four). It replaced the earlier 'no-frills' account.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A 'small account' under simplified KYC norms is valid for:
o: 12 months with caps on balance, credits and withdrawals
questions.e: Small accounts (self-certified KYC) operate for 12 months, extendable by 12 more months if the customer provides OVDs. Caps: balance ₹50,000, aggregate credits ₹1 lakh/year, withdrawals ₹10,000/month.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Nomination facility under the Banking Regulation Act is available for:
o: Deposits, safe custody articles and lockers
questions.e: Sections 45ZA–45ZF of the BR Act provide nomination for deposits, articles in safe custody and safe-deposit lockers. The nominee receives the asset as a trustee for the legal heirs.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Deposits not operated for 10 years or more are transferred to:
o: The bank's profit and loss account
The Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF) with the RBI
questions.e: Unclaimed deposits (10+ years inoperative) go to DEAF, maintained by the RBI. The depositor (or legal heir) can still claim the amount from the bank with interest.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: In a loan account, the banker–customer relationship is:
questions.e: The relationship inverts with the product: in deposit accounts the bank is the debtor, while in loan accounts the bank is the creditor and the customer the debtor.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A person who only purchases a demand draft without holding an account is:
o: A full customer of the bank
Not a customer in the full sense, though the bank owes transaction duties
questions.e: The durable banker–customer relationship arises from an account contract. Casual users of services like DD purchase get transaction-specific duties but not the full relationship (e.g. no lien on their other assets).

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The banker's general lien does NOT extend to:
o: Securities against which a loan is outstanding
Bills left for collection with a general mandate
Securities deposited for a special purpose or safe custody
questions.e: Section 171's general lien covers goods/securities in the bank's possession in the ordinary course of banking for the general balance due — but not items held for a special purpose or in safe custody.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: For the right of set-off, the accounts combined must be:
o: In the same name and same right/capacity
In any names at the same branch
Joint and sole accounts freely mixed
questions.e: Set-off requires mutuality — the same customer in the same capacity (e.g. a sole account cannot be set off against a trust account where the customer is trustee). Due notice to the customer is required.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: When a cheque is collected as an agent for the customer, the relationship is:
questions.e: In collection of cheques and execution of standing instructions, the bank acts as the customer's agent. Until the proceeds are credited, the agency relationship governs.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Safe deposit locker hiring creates which relationship?
questions.e: Locker hiring is a lease of space (lessor–lessee); the bank does not know the contents. Safe custody of sealed packets is bailment (bailor–bailee). This distinction matters for the bank's liability.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: On receiving notice of a customer's death, the bank should:
o: Immediately distribute the balance to heirs
Close the account the same day
Stop operations in the account pending the claim settlement
questions.e: Notice of death terminates the customer's mandate; cheques signed before death but presented after should not be paid. The balance is settled to the nominee/survivor or legal heirs.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Cheques drawn by a customer before death but presented after the bank receives notice of death:
o: Should be referred to the RBI
questions.e: Death terminates the agency/mandate, so the bank has no authority to debit the account after notice of death. Payment after notice would not be 'payment in due course'.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A partnership firm's account is operated as per:
o: The partnership deed / mandate and the law of agency
questions.e: A firm has no separate legal personality; partners are agents of the firm. The account mandate flows from the partnership deed, and death/insolvency of a partner affects operations unless the deed provides otherwise.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: For opening a company's account, the bank must obtain:
o: Board resolution authorising account opening and operators
questions.e: A company acts through its board; the bank needs a certified board resolution naming authorised signatories, plus the certificate of incorporation, MOA/AOA and KYC of authorised persons.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The RBI deregulated interest rates on savings bank deposits in:
questions.e: Savings deposit rates were deregulated in October 2011, letting banks set their own rates (most pay quarterly or as per their policy).

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Current accounts are meant for:
o: Business entities with frequent transactions; no interest is paid
questions.e: Current accounts suit businesses with heavy transaction volumes; no interest is payable, and banks may levy service charges. Individuals can also open them for business purposes.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Banks are required to disclose the penal charge on premature withdrawal of a term deposit:
o: At the time of opening the deposit itself
Never — it is at the bank's discretion
questions.e: RBI requires the penal interest policy on premature withdrawal to be disclosed upfront at account opening and in the terms of the deposit.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The 'either or survivor' mandate is an example of:
o: A nomination under the BR Act
A contractual term between the bank and joint holders
questions.e: Survivorship mandates are contractual; nomination is a separate statutory facility under Sections 45ZA–45ZF. Both can coexist — the mandate governs operations, nomination governs settlement after death.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Standing instructions from a customer create:
o: An agency relationship for recurring payments
questions.e: Standing instructions (EMI debits, utility payments, fund transfers) make the bank the customer's agent. They continue until revoked and lapse on notice of death.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: KYC for politically exposed persons (PEPs) requires:
o: Enhanced due diligence and senior management approval
questions.e: PEPs (and high-risk customers generally) attract enhanced due diligence: deeper background checks, senior management sign-off for the relationship, and closer transaction monitoring.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Record of transactions under PMLA must be maintained for:
o: 5 years from the date of transaction / end of business relationship
questions.e: Reporting entities must preserve transaction records for five years from the transaction date and KYC records for five years after the business relationship ends, available to FIU-IND and enforcement agencies.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Cash transactions of what value must banks report to FIU-IND as CTRs?
o: ₹10 lakh and above in a month (aggregate)
questions.e: Cash Transaction Reports cover all cash transactions above ₹10 lakh, or integrally connected cash transactions aggregating to ₹10 lakh+ in a month. STRs have no monetary threshold.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Aadhaar-based e-KYC for account opening uses:
o: OTP or biometric authentication against UIDAI data
questions.e: e-KYC verifies identity through UIDAI authentication (OTP to the registered mobile or biometrics). Offline Aadhaar XML and V-CIP are alternatives where e-KYC is not feasible.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Unique Customer Identification Code (UCIC) is intended to:
o: Give each customer a single identifier across all relationships with the bank
questions.e: UCIC lets banks view all accounts, loans and services of one customer together — aiding KYC, risk management and fraud detection. The 2024 KYC amendments pushed CDD at UCIC level.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: If a customer changes address, the bank must:
o: Ignore it until re-KYC falls due
Obtain fresh address proof and update KYC/CKYCR records
Charge a fee and do nothing
questions.e: Address change triggers KYC updation and CKYCR update within the prescribed time. Banks may accept a self-declaration for the new address with verification later, per RBI norms.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Non-face-to-face onboarding of customers is permitted through:
questions.e: The RBI allows remote onboarding via Video-CIP and e-KYC, subject to prescribed safeguards — expanding inclusion while keeping identity verification robust.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The June 2025 RBI KYC amendment requires, for periodic updation:
o: At least three advance intimations including one by letter
questions.e: Effective 1 January 2026, banks must send at least three intimations before the re-KYC due date (including one by letter) and three reminders after, recording each communication for audit.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A term deposit receipt is:
o: An acknowledgement of deposit, not a negotiable instrument
A negotiable instrument like a cheque
questions.e: A TDR merely evidences the deposit contract; it is not transferable by endorsement like a cheque. Some banks issue transferable CDs, but ordinary TDRs are non-negotiable.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Interest on a savings account of an NRI is paid in:
o: NRE/NRO accounts as per the account's terms
questions.e: NRIs maintain NRE (repatriable), NRO (non-repatriable income) and FCNR(B) deposits. NRE/FCNR interest is tax-free in India; NRO interest is taxable. This is a favourite exam distractor.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Recurring deposits are best described as:
o: Monthly instalments building a lump sum at maturity
questions.e: RDs suit small savers: fixed monthly instalments earn term-deposit-like interest, maturing into a lump sum. Premature closure follows term-deposit penal rules.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The bank's obligation to honour a customer's cheque arises from:
o: The contractual account relationship and sufficient collected balance
questions.e: Honouring cheques is part of the account contract, conditional on sufficient collected (not merely deposited) funds, proper drawing, and no legal bar such as a garnishee order or stop payment.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Unclaimed deposits remain claimable by the depositor:
o: No, they vest with the RBI permanently
Yes, from the bank with applicable interest, even after transfer to DEAF
questions.e: Transfer to DEAF does not extinguish the depositor's right; the bank remains liable to pay the depositor/legal heir with interest, and claims it back from the Fund.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) account is operated by:
o: Only the eldest male member's wife
The karta, as per the mandate
questions.e: The karta manages the HUF and operates its account; on the karta's death, the senior-most coparcener typically becomes karta. The HUF has a PAN and is assessed as a separate entity.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under the NI Act, 1881, a cheque is defined in:
questions.e: Section 6 defines a cheque as a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and payable on demand. Section 4 covers promissory notes and Section 5 bills of exchange; Section 10 defines payment in due course.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A promissory note is defined under which section of the NI Act?
questions.e: Section 4 defines a promissory note — a written promise by the maker to pay a certain sum to a certain person. It has two parties and cannot be made payable to bearer.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A bill of exchange is defined under which section of the NI Act?
questions.e: Section 5 defines a bill of exchange — an unconditional order by the drawer to the drawee to pay a certain person. Unlike a cheque it can be usance (payable after a period).

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: How many parties are there in a promissory note?
questions.e: A promissory note has the maker (promisor) and the payee. A bill of exchange and a cheque have three parties: drawer, drawee and payee.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A cheque is always:
questions.e: By definition (Section 6) a cheque is payable on demand; it cannot be a usance instrument. A post-dated cheque becomes payable on the date written on it.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The validity of cheques in India was reduced from 6 months to 3 months with effect from:
questions.e: RBI directed that cheques, drafts and banker's cheques are valid for 3 months from the date of issue with effect from 1 April 2012.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Negotiation of an order instrument is done by:
questions.e: Bearer instruments pass by mere delivery; order instruments require the holder's endorsement plus delivery. Endorsement is defined in Sections 15–16 of the NI Act.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A blank endorsement:
o: Consists of the endorser's signature only and makes the instrument bearer
questions.e: In a blank (general) endorsement the endorser merely signs; the instrument becomes payable to bearer. A special/full endorsement names the endorsee, keeping it an order instrument.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A 'sans recours' endorsement means:
o: The endorser excludes his liability on the instrument
The instrument is payable only in cash
questions.e: Sans recours (without recourse) endorsement lets the endorser transfer title while excluding personal liability if the instrument is dishonoured. A conditional endorsement makes liability depend on a specified event.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: General crossing of a cheque is defined in which section?
questions.e: Sections 123–131A deal with crossing: 123 (general crossing — two parallel transverse lines), 124 (special crossing naming a banker), 130 ('not negotiable'), 131 (collecting banker protection).

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: 'Not negotiable' crossing under Section 130 means:
o: The cheque cannot be transferred at all
The bank must not pay it
The transferee gets no better title than the transferor
questions.e: 'Not negotiable' takes away negotiability, not transferability — the holder in due course protection is lost, so a thief's transferee gets no title. It does not stop the cheque being transferred.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: 'Account payee' crossing on a cheque directs:
o: Credit of the proceeds only to the payee's account
Payment in cash across the counter
questions.e: A/c payee crossing (not in the statute but binding in practice) mandates credit to the named payee's account. Collecting it for another person is negligence, losing Section 131 protection.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Section 85 of the Negotiable Instruments Act gives protection to:
o: The collecting banker of a crossed cheque
The paying banker who pays an order cheque in due course
The endorser of a bearer cheque
questions.e: Section 85(1) protects a drawee banker who pays an order cheque in due course; Section 10 defines 'payment in due course'.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds is an offence under:
questions.e: Section 138 criminalises dishonour for insufficiency/exceeding arrangement, provided: written demand notice within 30 days of dishonour, 15 days to pay, and complaint within one month thereafter.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under Section 138, the payee must send the demand notice within:
questions.e: The cause of action under Section 138 needs: (1) written demand within 30 days of return, (2) 15 days for the drawer to pay, (3) complaint within one month of the cause of action arising.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The 2018 amendment to Section 138 introduced:
o: Interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount during trial
questions.e: Section 143A (2018 amendment) lets courts order the drawer to pay interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount to the complainant during trial, and Section 148 provides for deposit on appeal.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The collecting banker's statutory protection is in:
questions.e: Section 131 protects a collecting banker that collects a crossed cheque in good faith and without negligence for a customer with title or apparent title. Negligence — e.g. collecting an A/c payee cheque for a stranger — destroys the protection.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The paying banker's protection for forged endorsements is in:
questions.e: Section 85 protects the drawee paying a cheque in due course even if the endorsement is forged, and Section 89 covers payment per apparent tenor despite material alteration not being apparent.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: If the amount in words and figures on a cheque differ, the bank should pay:
questions.e: Section 18 of the NI Act: where the amount in words and figures differ, the amount stated in words prevails. This is a classic exam one-marker.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A material alteration to a cheque:
o: Voids it against non-consenting parties under Section 87
questions.e: Section 87: material alteration (amount, date, payee, crossing) without the consent of all liable parties voids the instrument against them. The bank must not pay an altered cheque.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A demand draft differs from a cheque because:
o: It is valid for one year
The bank is both drawer and drawee, and it cannot be countermanded
It is always payable to bearer
questions.e: A DD is drawn by a bank on its own branch/office; the purchaser cannot stop its payment (unlike a cheque). DDs are valid for 3 months like cheques.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Stop-payment instructions on a cheque:
o: Must be obeyed by the bank if received before payment
Can be ignored by the bank
questions.e: A drawer's countermand is a lawful instruction; paying after receiving it (with reasonable time to act) makes the bank liable. The instruction should identify the cheque precisely.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Cheque Truncation System (CTS) in India is managed by:
questions.e: NPCI operates CTS, which replaced physical cheque movement with electronic images + MICR data. Only CTS-2010 standard cheques are processed; non-CTS cheques were discontinued.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: CTS-2010 standard cheques became mandatory because:
o: RBI directed migration for standardised security features
questions.e: The RBI mandated CTS-2010 cheques with standardised security features (watermark, VOID pantograph). Non-CTS cheques were fully discontinued from end-2018.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Positive Pay System was introduced by the RBI from:
questions.e: PPS (1 January 2021) requires the issuer to share cheque details (date, payee, amount) electronically for cheques of ₹50,000 and above; banks may make it mandatory for ₹5 lakh and above. NPCI built the facility on CTS.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under Positive Pay, banks may make the facility mandatory for cheques of:
questions.e: RBI: banks must enable PPS for all account holders issuing cheques of ₹50,000+; availing is at the holder's discretion, but banks may make it mandatory for ₹5 lakh+. Only PPS-compliant cheques get CTS dispute-resolution cover.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: MICR code on a cheque is used for:
o: Encoding the cheque amount in words
High-speed electronic sorting and processing of cheques
questions.e: Magnetic Ink Character Recognition prints the 9-digit code (city-bank-branch) in magnetic ink, enabling fast automated sorting in clearing houses and CTS.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A 'stale' cheque is one:
questions.e: A stale cheque has crossed its validity and must be returned. A post-dated cheque bears a future date and is payable only on/after that date; an ante-dated cheque bears an earlier date and is valid.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which endorsement makes a cheque payable to bearer?
questions.e: A blank endorsement (signature only) converts an order cheque into a bearer cheque. A special endorsement names the endorsee; restrictive ('pay X only') limits further negotiation.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A cheque crossed 'not negotiable' and 'A/c payee':
o: Can still be transferred, but the transferee gets no better title and proceeds must go to the payee's account
questions.e: The two crossings combine: 'not negotiable' kills holder-in-due-course protection; 'A/c payee' restricts credit to the payee's account. Transfer remains legally possible.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The drawee of a cheque is:
o: The bank on which it is drawn
questions.e: Drawer = account holder who signs; drawee = the bank ordered to pay; payee = recipient. In a DD, the bank is both drawer and drawee.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A usance bill of exchange:
o: Is the same as a cheque
Is payable after a specified period
questions.e: Usance (time) bills are payable after a tenor (e.g. 90 days after sight). Demand bills are payable on presentation. Cheques, being demand instruments, cannot be usance.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Days of grace for a usance bill are:
questions.e: A usance bill maturing on a date gets three days of grace before payment is due (if the third day is a holiday, payment is due the preceding business day). Demand instruments get no grace.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Inchoate (incomplete) stamped instruments are covered by:
questions.e: Section 20 lets the holder of a signed-but-incomplete stamped instrument complete it up to the stamp-covered amount. This underpins blank signed cheques given as security.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A cheque drawn by a company must be signed:
o: By authorised signatories as per the board resolution
questions.e: Companies act through authorised signatories named in a board resolution; the bank verifies signatures against the recorded mandate. Ultra vires or unauthorised signatures do not bind the company.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The bank must verify before paying a cheque:
o: Signature, date, amount in words/figures, alterations, stop-payment and sufficient balance
questions.e: The paying banker's checklist: genuine signature, valid date (not stale/post-dated before date), words/figures agreement, no material alteration, no stop-payment/garnishee, and sufficient collected funds.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Collecting an 'A/c payee' cheque for someone other than the named payee is:
questions.e: A/c payee crossing mandates credit to the payee's account. Collecting for another person is negligence per se, so the bank loses statutory protection and faces conversion liability.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A forged drawer's signature on a cheque:
o: Gives no title; the bank paying it bears the loss
Can be ratified by the payee
questions.e: A forged signature is wholly inoperative — the mandate never existed. Unlike a forged endorsement (Section 85 protects payment in due course), a forged drawer signature leaves the loss with the paying bank.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Speed clearing of cheques refers to:
o: Collection of outstation cheques through the CTS grid
questions.e: Speed clearing uses the CTS infrastructure to collect outstation cheques quickly, replacing the old slow outstation collection process.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The return of a dishonoured cheque must be accompanied by:
o: A return memo with the standardised reason code
questions.e: Banks return unpaid cheques with a return memo citing standardised reason codes (e.g. insufficient funds, signature mismatch). Repeated dishonour of high-value cheques can lead to account closure after notice.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under Section 138, which debt is covered?
o: A legally enforceable debt or liability
questions.e: Section 138 needs a legally enforceable debt. Time-barred debts, gifts and illegal (e.g. wagering) debts do not attract liability — a favourite exam trap.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: An 'order cheque' is payable to:
o: The named payee or his order
questions.e: Order cheques are payable to the named payee or as he orders (by endorsement). Bearer cheques are payable to whoever presents them — riskier if lost.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Crossing can be done by:
o: The drawer, holder or the collecting banker
questions.e: The drawer may cross at issue; the holder may add crossing; a banker may cross specially to itself as collecting agent. Crossing is a direction to pay through a banker.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Once a cheque is crossed specially, it can be crossed again:
o: Only specially to the collecting banker as agent for collection
questions.e: Section 124 permits re-crossing a specially crossed cheque only to the banker collecting as agent. A general crossing may be converted into a special crossing.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The liability of the drawer of a cheque is:
o: Primary, as he promises the bank will pay
questions.e: The drawer is primarily liable to the holder if the cheque is dishonoured (after due notice). Endorsers have secondary liability, arising only on dishonour after notice.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Notice of dishonour to the drawer is:
o: Necessary to fix liability, except where excused
questions.e: Notice of dishonour fixes the drawer's/endorser's liability; it is excused when the drawer cannot be found, or has countermanded payment, among other cases in Sections 98–104.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A bill drawn in India and payable outside India is:
questions.e: Section 11–12: inland bills are drawn and payable in India (or drawn in India on a resident); others are foreign bills, attracting different stamp and protest rules.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Protest for dishonour is:
o: A notarial certificate of dishonour, mainly for foreign bills
questions.e: Protest (Sections 100–104) is a notary's certificate evidencing dishonour, giving better proof than mere noting. It is mainly used for foreign bills; noting is the preliminary minute.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The holder in due course must have taken the instrument:
o: For consideration, in good faith, before maturity, without notice of defect
questions.e: Section 9: a holder in due course takes for value, in good faith, before overdue, without notice of title defects — and then gets a title free from prior defects, even from a thief.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under Section 138, after the 15-day payment window expires without payment, the complaint must be filed within:
questions.e: The Section 138 timeline is strict: demand notice within 30 days of dishonour, 15 days for the drawer to pay, and the complaint within one month of the cause of action. Courts may condone delay only on sufficient cause.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the 5 Cs of credit appraisal?
questions.e: The 5 Cs are Character, Capacity, Capital, Collateral and Conditions — 'Commission' is not among them.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: CAMEL rating of banks covers:
o: Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity
questions.e: CAMEL (plus S for Systems/Sensitivity) is the supervisory rating framework. Asset quality captures NPAs; management and earnings capture governance and profitability.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Chore Committee (1979) is associated with:
o: A review of the cash-credit system of working-capital finance
questions.e: The Chore Committee reviewed the working-capital cash-credit system and recommended discipline in utilisation, following up the Tandon Committee norms.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Nayak Committee recommended for small borrowers:
o: Working capital as 20% of projected turnover, with 5% margin
questions.e: The Nayak Committee's turnover method: banks may sanction working capital up to 20% of projected annual turnover, with the borrower bringing 5% as margin — simple and suited to small units.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Cash credit is:
o: A running account facility against stock/receivables, renewed annually
questions.e: Cash credit is a revolving working-capital limit secured by hypothecation of stock and book debts, with annual review/renewal. Interest is charged on the utilised amount.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: An overdraft differs from cash credit mainly in that:
o: It is usually granted against securities or clean, often for short periods
questions.e: Overdrafts allow overdrawing a current account up to a limit, typically against financial securities or clean (temporary), while cash credit is the structured working-capital facility against current assets.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Pledge under the Indian Contract Act is defined in:
o: Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act
Section 130 of the Transfer of Property Act
questions.e: Section 172 defines pledge (pawnor/pledgee) — bailment of goods as security with possession passing to the bank. Section 171 is the banker's lien; mortgage is Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The contract of pledge is defined under:
o: Section 171 of the Indian Contract Act
Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act
questions.e: Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines pledge as bailment of goods as security; Section 171 covers the banker's general lien.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Mortgage of immovable property is defined in:
o: Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882
Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act
questions.e: Section 58 defines mortgage as transfer of interest in immovable property to secure a loan. Types: simple, usufructuary, English, mortgage by conditional sale, equitable (deposit of title deeds), and anomalous.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Equitable mortgage is created by:
o: Deposit of title deeds in a notified town
questions.e: Mortgage by deposit of title deeds needs no registered instrument where the town is notified under Section 58(f). It is cheap and quick — hence popular for housing loans — but CERSAI registration is now required.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Assignment of an LIC policy as security is governed by:
o: Section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act
Section 172 of the Indian Contract Act
Section 130 of the Transfer of Property Act (actionable claims)
questions.e: LIC policies and book debts are actionable claims assigned under Section 130, with written notice to the debtor/insurer. The assignee steps into the assignor's shoes.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: CERSAI registration is required for:
o: Security interests over property to prevent multiple financing
questions.e: The Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest (CERSAI) records mortgages and hypothecation so lenders can detect prior charges — a key anti-fraud check.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A demand promissory note must be kept alive within:
o: 3 years, through acknowledgement or balance confirmation
questions.e: Under the Limitation Act, 1963, a DPN is enforceable for 3 years; Sections 18–19 extend limitation on written acknowledgement of debt or part-payment. Banks obtain annual balance confirmations.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: An asset is classified as NPA when interest/instalment remains overdue for more than:
questions.e: The 90-day delinquency norm: term-loan instalments, cash-credit/OD out-of-order status, or bills overdue beyond 90 days make the account NPA. Agricultural norms follow crop seasons.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A sub-standard asset attracts a provision of:
questions.e: Sub-standard (NPA up to 12 months): 15% on the secured portion, 25% if the exposure is unsecured. Doubtful assets attract 25%/40%/100% on the secured portion by age slab plus 100% of unsecured; loss assets 100%.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Doubtful assets are provided for at:
o: 25%, 40% and 100% on the secured portion by age slab, plus 100% of unsecured
questions.e: Doubtful-1 (up to 1 year): 25%; Doubtful-2 (1–3 years): 40%; Doubtful-3 (3+ years): 100% — on the realisable secured portion, with 100% on the unsecured portion throughout.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A loan account in India is classified as NPA when interest or instalment remains overdue for more than:
questions.e: The 90-days-past-due norm applies to term loans, cash credit and bills; farm credit has season-based norms.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The SARFAESI Act was enacted in:
questions.e: SARFAESI (2002) lets secured creditors enforce security interest without court intervention: 60-day demand notice under Section 13(2), then possession/sale under 13(4). It does not apply to agricultural land.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under SARFAESI, the borrower must be given what notice period before enforcement?
questions.e: Section 13(2) requires a 60-day demand notice. On non-compliance, the creditor may take possession, sell or manage the secured asset under Section 13(4); the borrower can appeal to the DRT.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Appeal against SARFAESI action lies with the DRT on deposit of:
questions.e: Section 17 appeals to the DRT need a pre-deposit of 50% of the debt due, which the tribunal may reduce to 25% for reasons recorded. Further appeal lies to the DRAT.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Debt Recovery Tribunals were set up under:
questions.e: The Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 created DRTs/DRATs for speedy adjudication of bank dues of ₹20 lakh and above (threshold revised over time).

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 provides:
o: A time-bound 180+90 day resolution process through the NCLT
questions.e: IBC consolidated insolvency law with a creditor-in-control model: 180 days (extendable by 90) for resolution, failing which liquidation. The Committee of Creditors votes on resolution plans.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The SARFAESI Act can be invoked by a secured creditor only where the amount due is:
questions.e: SARFAESI applies to debts of Rs.1 lakh and above that are classified as NPAs; it does not apply to agricultural land.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under RBI's wilful-defaulter framework, the Identification Committee that labels a borrower a wilful defaulter is headed by:
o: An Executive Director (or equivalent) of the bank
questions.e: The Identification Committee is headed by an Executive Director or equivalent; its finding is reviewed by a higher Review Committee headed by the Chairman/CEO.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The overall priority-sector lending target for domestic commercial banks is:
questions.e: Domestic banks must lend 40% of ANBC to priority sectors; within this, 18% is the sub-target for agriculture.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Priority sector sub-target for micro enterprises is:
questions.e: Micro enterprises carry a 7.5% sub-target of ANBC for domestic banks. PSLC–Micro Enterprises certificates let surplus banks sell this achievement to deficit banks.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Priority sector sub-target for weaker sections for domestic banks is:
questions.e: Weaker sections (small/marginal farmers, artisans, SC/ST, SHGs, etc.) have a 12% sub-target for domestic banks and 15% for RRBs. Shortfalls attract RIDF deposits.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: PSLCs are:
o: Tradable certificates letting surplus banks sell PSL achievement to deficit banks
questions.e: Priority Sector Lending Certificates (Agriculture, SF/Marginal Farmer, Micro Enterprises, General) trade on RBI platforms. PSLC General cannot offset sub-target shortfalls — only the overall target.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Shortfall in PSL targets is parked in:
o: RIDF with NABARD (and funds with SIDBI/NHB)
questions.e: Banks missing PSL targets contribute the shortfall to the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (agriculture shortfall) or funds with SIDBI/NHB, earning low interest — a real cost of non-compliance.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: MUDRA loans are given to:
o: Non-corporate, non-farm micro/small enterprises for income-generating activities
questions.e: PMMY (8 April 2015) funds the unfunded through banks, NBFCs and MFIs for manufacturing, trading, services and allied agriculture — not to corporates or farm operations directly.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Under MUDRA, the 'Kishor' category covers loans:
questions.e: Shishu: up to ₹50,000; Kishor: ₹50,000–₹5 lakh; Tarun: ₹5–₹10 lakh; Tarun Plus: ₹10–₹20 lakh (for those who repaid Tarun loans, effective 24 October 2024).

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Tarun Plus under MUDRA is available to:
o: Entrepreneurs who have availed and successfully repaid a Tarun loan
questions.e: Announced in Budget 2024-25 and effective 24 October 2024, Tarun Plus (₹10–₹20 lakh) rewards successful Tarun borrowers, with CGFMU guarantee cover extended to ₹20 lakh.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Stand-Up India (2016) mandates per bank branch:
o: Loans of ₹10 lakh–₹1 crore to at least one SC/ST and one woman borrower
questions.e: Stand-Up India promotes greenfield enterprises by SC/ST and women entrepreneurs with bank loans of ₹10 lakh to ₹1 crore, backed by NCGTC guarantee and RuPay debit cards.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Kisan Credit Card was introduced in:
questions.e: KCC (1998, on R.V. Gupta Committee recommendation) meets crop cultivation, maintenance and allied-activity needs with interest subvention for prompt repayment; it now covers animal husbandry and fisheries too.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The SHG–Bank Linkage Programme began in:
questions.e: NABARD's 1992 pilot linking self-help groups to banks became the world's largest microfinance programme, especially empowering rural women through group lending.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A letter of credit is:
o: A bank's undertaking to pay the seller if documents comply
questions.e: An LC is a non-fund-based facility: the issuing bank promises to pay the beneficiary against complying documents. Types include revocable/irrevocable, confirmed, standby and revolving LCs.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A bank guarantee is:
o: A non-fund-based commitment to pay if the customer defaults
questions.e: Financial guarantees back monetary obligations; performance guarantees back contract execution. The bank pays only on invocation — hence 'non-fund-based' — but must assess like a loan.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Bills purchased/discounted by banks are:
questions.e: Discounting/purchasing bills gives the seller immediate funds against the buyer's acceptance — fund-based exposure on the drawee. Usance bills carry a tenor; demand bills are payable on presentation.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: A debt-service coverage ratio consistently below 1 indicates that the borrower:
o: Lacks sufficient cash accruals to service its debt
questions.e: DSCR = cash accruals available for debt service / debt obligations; below 1 means accruals cannot cover interest plus instalments.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Break-even analysis finds:
o: The sales level with no profit and no loss
questions.e: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit (or P/V ratio). It tells lenders the minimum scale at which the project survives — vital for term-loan appraisal.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Working capital is:
questions.e: Net working capital = CA − CL. The operating cycle (inventory + receivables − payables days) drives working-capital need; banks fund the gap after the borrower's margin.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The operating cycle of a business is:
o: Inventory days + receivable days − payable days
questions.e: The operating cycle measures cash locked in operations. Longer cycles need more working capital — the logic behind Tandon/Chore norms and MPBF computation.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Margin on advances against shares is prescribed because:
o: Share prices are volatile, so a cushion protects the bank
questions.e: Margins (haircuts) protect against price falls; the RBI prescribes minimum margins for advances against shares and sensitive commodities — a qualitative credit-control tool.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Restructuring of advances is governed by:
o: The RBI's prudential framework for resolution of stressed assets
questions.e: The June 2019 prudential framework requires early recognition, independent credit evaluation for large exposures, and inter-creditor agreements — with additional provisioning for delays.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Compromise settlement of NPAs:
o: Needs RBI approval in every case
Is a commercial decision within the bank's board-approved policy
questions.e: Banks may compromise/settle NPAs as a commercial call under board policy, weighing recovery cost and time. Wilful defaulters and fraud cases face restrictions on compromise.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: The Securitisation of stressed assets is done through:
o: ARCs issuing security receipts to qualified buyers
questions.e: Asset Reconstruction Companies (SARFAESI-registered) buy NPAs from banks and issue security receipts to qualified institutional buyers; NARCL (the 'bad bank') handles large exposures.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Priority sector includes which of the following?
o: Agriculture, MSME, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy, export credit, others
questions.e: Eight PSL categories: agriculture, MSME, export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy and others (SHGs, weaker sections, etc.). Large industry is not priority sector.

questions.subject: DBF
questions.q: Education loans up to the prescribed limit qualify as:
questions.e: Education loans (up to ₹10 lakh in India / ₹20 lakh abroad under older caps; limits revised periodically) to individuals qualify as priority sector, supporting the social objective.

questions.subject: DBF
